Hierarchical time series are time series that can be divided into sub-series.
In `persephone3`, such objects are created similar to a nested list. The
following example creates a series with European aggregates based on export data from different European countries.

First we load the `Exports` data from `rjd3toolkit`:
```{r}
library(persephone3)

data(Exports, package = "rjd3toolkit")
```

For all countries' time series we now want to generate a persephone object with Tramo as method.

```{r}
# Selected countries available in this dataset (26 series; Belgium is absent)
eu_countries <- c("France", "Luxembourg", "Netherlands", "Germany", "Italy",
                  "Ireland", "Denmark", "Greece", "Portugal",
                  "Spain", "Sweden", "Finland", "Austria", "Malta", "Estonia",
                  "Latvia", "Lithuania", "Poland", "Czech.Republic", "Slovakia",
                  "Hungary", "Slovenia", "Cyprus", "Bulgaria", "Romania", "Croatia")

country_series <- lapply(Exports[eu_countries], perTramo)
```

We generate an additional layer based on a certain regional grouping of the countries.

```{r}
# Define regional groupings using the actual country names from the dataset
south_eastern_europe <- c("Greece", "Cyprus", "Bulgaria", "Romania")
northern_europe <- c("Denmark", "Finland", "Sweden", "Ireland")
central_europe <- c("Croatia", "Germany", "Czech.Republic", "Slovakia", "Hungary",
                    "Austria", "Slovenia", "Luxembourg", "Estonia", "Lithuania",
                    "Latvia", "Poland")
southern_europe <- c("Italy", "Spain", "Portugal", "Malta")
western_europe <- c("France", "Netherlands")
```

The list argument can be used to create a hierarchical persephone object based on a list of persephone objects.

```{r}
hts_see <- perHts(list = country_series[south_eastern_europe])
hts_ne <- perHts(list = country_series[northern_europe])
hts_ce <- perHts(list = country_series[central_europe])
hts_se <- perHts(list = country_series[southern_europe])
hts_we <- perHts(list = country_series[western_europe])
```


An additional layer is only the northern part and southern part
```{r}
hts_np <- perHts(northern_europe = hts_ne,
                 western_europe = hts_we,
                 central_europe = hts_ce
)
hts_sp <- perHts(southern_europe = hts_se,
                 south_eastern_europe = hts_see
)
```

Finally we aggregate the selected countries. This illustrative grouping is not
a complete EU aggregate.
```{r}
ht_europe <- perHts(north_part = hts_np,
                 south_part = hts_sp
)
ht_europe
```

Now we make the first run:
```{r}
ht_europe$run()
ht_europe
```


# Weights

Weights change aggregation from a sum to a weighted mean. This is useful when the time series are indices. Named weights are matched to component names; varying weights retain their historical values and extend only their final value beyond the supplied history.

## Time-invariant weights

The weights parameter will be set as numeric vector with length equal to the number of components.

Almost the same call, but with weights, one for each component.
```{r}
hts_see <- perHts(list = country_series[south_eastern_europe], weights=c(1,2,3,4))
hts_ne <- perHts(list = country_series[northern_europe], weights = c(5,6,7,8)) # 4 countries: Denmark, Finland, Sweden, Ireland
hts_ce <- perHts(list = country_series[central_europe], weights = rep(1,12))
hts_se <- perHts(list = country_series[southern_europe], weights = c(8,9,10,10.5))
hts_we <- perHts(list = country_series[western_europe], weights = c(11,12)) # 2 countries: France, Netherlands
```

In additional aggregation steps, the weight is automatically summed up. So e.g. the weight for central europe is 12, the sum of 12 times 1.
```{r}
hts_np <- perHts(northern_europe = hts_ne,
                 western_europe = hts_we,
                 central_europe = hts_ce
)
hts_sp <- perHts(southern_europe = hts_se,
                 south_eastern_europe = hts_see
)
knitr::kable(head(hts_np$weights))
```


```{r}
ht_europe <- perHts(north_part = hts_np,
                 south_part = hts_sp
)

knitr::kable(head(ht_europe$weights))
```


## Time-variant weights

In many scenarios weights are not fixed over time, but change, e.g. if the turnover is used to aggregate a certain production index. In these scenarios weights can be provided as lists of time series or as a mts object.

We are starting with weights equal to 1 and then only change the weight of Germany over time.

```{r}
# Convert list to mts (multi-time series) object
weights_eu <- do.call(cbind, Exports[eu_countries]) * 0 + 1
weights_eu[is.na(weights_eu)] <- 1
set.seed(123)
weights_eu[,"Germany"] <- weights_eu[,"Germany"] + rlnorm(nrow(weights_eu))
```


We can now call the `perHts` function with the mts as input.
```{r}
hts_see <- perHts(list = country_series[south_eastern_europe],
                   weights=weights_eu[,south_eastern_europe])
hts_ne <- perHts(list = country_series[northern_europe],
                  weights=weights_eu[,northern_europe])
hts_ce <- perHts(list = country_series[central_europe],
                  weights=weights_eu[,central_europe])
hts_se <- perHts(list = country_series[southern_europe],
                  weights=weights_eu[,southern_europe])
hts_we <- perHts(list = country_series[western_europe],
                  weights=weights_eu[,western_europe])
```

And then we can proceed as before.

```{r}
hts_np <- perHts(northern_europe = hts_ne,
                 western_europe = hts_we,
                 central_europe = hts_ce
)
hts_sp <- perHts(southern_europe = hts_se,
                 south_eastern_europe = hts_see
)
knitr::kable(head(hts_np$weights))
```


```{r}
ht_europe <- perHts(north_part = hts_np,
                 south_part = hts_sp
)

knitr::kable(head(ht_europe$weights))
```
